issue_context.body:
### What would you like to be added?

The `test/e2e` tests are full of assertions which compare a boolean against true or false, often without any additional explanation. When those assertions fail, the error message is useless for understanding what went wrong, often just saying:
```
      Apr 22 09:03:41.130: Expected
          <bool>: false
      to equal
          <bool>: true
```

Including an explanation is better, but then we still have the distracting noise about the comparison:
```
      Apr 22 09:08:49.598: Failed to do XYZ
      Expected
          <bool>: false
      to equal
          <bool>: true
```

All of those assertions should be replace with `if (<failure check>) framework.Failf(<informative message>)`.

Such locations can be found by grepping:
```
$ git grep 'Expect.*Equal([^,]*, *\(true\|false\)' | wc -l
272
```

UPDATE (2024-08-26): in cases where such an if check is not possible (typically in combination with `gomega.Eventually` or `gomega.Consistently`), `gomega.Be[False/True]Because` should be used instead of `gomega.Be[False/True]`. They emit only the explanation given to them, without including the noise above. The Ginkgo linter (enabled in golangci-lint) points that out.

Some progress has been made in the meantime:
- v1.23.0: 250
- v1.24.0-beta.0: 177

However, we were down to 175 at some point, so the number is going back up.

Example:
```
test/e2e/storage/vsphere/vsphere_volume_diskformat.go:  framework.ExpectEqual(isAttached, true)
=>
if (!isAttached) {
   framework.Failf("volume %s is not attached", ...)
}
```

Some other places compare values. Those should be replaced with a comparison assertion. Example:
```
test/e2e/upgrades/apps/etcd.go: framework.ExpectEqual(ratio > 0.75, true)
=>
gomega.Expect(ratio).To(gomega.BeNumerically(">", 0.75), "ratio too small")
```

It makes sense to split this work into individual PRs, one per OWNERS file under test/e2e. Here's a list of directories:
- [ ] test/e2e/apimachinery @hunknownz
- [x] test/e2e/apps: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/109944

xref https://go.dev/doc/faq#testing_framework

> Where is my favorite helper function for testing?
> Go's standard testing package makes it easy to write unit tests, but it lacks features provided in other language's testing frameworks such as assertion functions. An earlier section of this document explained why Go doesn't have assertions, and the same arguments apply to the use of assert in tests. Proper error handling means letting other tests run after one has failed, so that the person debugging the failure gets a complete picture of what is wrong. It is more useful for a test to report that isPrime gives the wrong answer for 2, 3, 5, and 7 (or for 2, 4, 8, and 16) than to report that isPrime gives the wrong answer for 2 and therefore no more tests were run. The programmer who triggers the test failure may not be familiar with the code that fails. Time invested writing a good error message now pays off later when the test breaks.
> 
> A related point is that testing frameworks tend to develop into mini-languages of their own, with conditionals and controls and printing mechanisms, but Go already has all those capabilities; why recreate them? We'd rather write tests in Go; it's one fewer language to learn and the approach keeps the tests straightforward and easy to understand.
> 
> If the amount of extra code required to write good errors seems repetitive and overwhelming, the test might work better if table-driven, iterating over a list of inputs and outputs defined in a data structure (Go has excellent support for data structure literals). The work to write a good test and good error messages will then be amortized over many test cases. The standard Go library is full of illustrative examples, such as in the formatting tests for the fmt package.

But not quite. What we have left now is checking a boolean via `gomega.BeTrue` or `gomega.BeFalse`, which has the same problem. In some cases, there is an extra message (which is still noisy, see https://github.com/onsi/gomega/issues/670), in other cases there isn't even that (which makes the failure message fairly useless).
